newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa mulls JSE listing for St Lucia wetlands.
newsitem.headline: South Africa mulls JSE listing for St Lucia wetlands.

text.p: South Africa is considering a listing on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange for Africa's largest system of estuaries as the Greater St Lucia Wetland Park Company, in a bid to make eco-tourism financially viable.
The company will be a partnership between the state Natal Parks Board and the privately owned Conservation Corporation which manages the luxury Londolozi and Phinda game reserves.

It is envisaged that black communities surrounding the park, including those who claim the wetlands as ancestral lands, and park staff may be allocated shares in the company. At least 400 jobs are expected to be created if the company is listed.
"It's unique anywhere in the world. We are very excited," the parks board's George Hughes told Reuters.
Wildlife experts are concerned that if no work opportunities are created in the job-starved Zulu heartland through eco-tourism, a recently banished threat of mining could return.
"We've got to deliver in the language people understand -- job creation and direct economic benefits," said Hughes.

Conservationists won the battle against titanium mining in St Lucia in March when the cabinet turned down a proposal by Richards Bay Minerals, owned half-half by South Africa's Gencor Ltd and Britain's Rio Tinto Zinc Corp Plc.

The Natal Parks Board, Conservation Corporation and French Development Bank have commissioned a feasibility study into the listing, which is under way. Once finalised, a survey of user rights in protected nature areas is planned.
"The structure of the company must still be decided, but the target for us to get off the ground is the end of 1997," Hughes added.
Conservation Corporation deputy chairman Alan Bernstein said they hoped to apply institutional capital to the development of a conservation area providing low impact, high quality tourism.

"It would be literally the only opportunity for institutions to invest heavily in an eco-tourism development scheme -- there are no other opportunities. The tourism industry in this country has not got itself structured to attract major capital.

"It's extremely early days (but) we hope that we can combine resources to facilitate institutional investment to come into the formation of a Greater St Lucia Wetlands Park Company, with capital provided by domestic investors," said Bernstein.

The parks board plans to maintain primary responsibility for conservation within the 2,200 square km (850 sq miles) St Lucia wetlands, home to the country's largest population of hippos, to protect its natural resources.
"We would like to avoid 'rent-and-ruin' economics. The company will manage anything which has revenue opportunities but conservation will remain in our hands," Hughes said.
